title: Investigating Reaction Time
question: How much do three responses vary in one setup, and what does a response-time measurement include?

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: Will three responses in the same setup have exactly the same time? Predict why they might vary. Does the whole task time measure only how fast a signal travels along one nerve?
blocks.text: I predict the three task intervals may vary because attention, preparation, movement and device timing can vary. The whole interval does not isolate travel along one nerve.

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: How will you keep the device, response method, hand position and task the same? Why should a press before the cue be excluded? What could still vary even with these controls?
blocks.text: Keep the device, response method, task and comfortable hand position the same. A press before the cue cannot measure a response to that cue. There are three repeated measurements of one setup, not three independent people.
Timing: Before pathway action or timed observations.
Response method: Pointer press · mouse, touch or pen.

Use one device and one chosen response method for all three observations. If using a pointer, keep the same mouse, touch or pen type. Keep your hand position comfortable and consistent. Wait for RESPOND to replace WAIT; do not guess a countdown. The interval before the cue varies. Text and color both identify the cue. This is one person’s repeated task in one setup, not three people or independent groups.

The retina detects light; signals travel toward the brain.
Correct after feedback.

Brain networks use the cue and the task rule to prepare a response.
Correct after feedback.

Signals travel through brain/spinal motor pathways toward hand muscles.
Correct after feedback.

Muscles act and the hand operates the response control.
Correct after feedback.

Source: browser cue-update callback to response-event handler, rounded to whole ms. These are on-device task measurements, not calibrated nerve travel times. Display/input/software delays are included. Valid trials: 3 of 3. Any pending trial has no elapsed result.

blocks.prompt: Trace the cue to sensory input, brain processing, motor signals and hand action. Why is this total task time different from the travel time along one nerve? How does following this task’s rule differ from a simple automatic reflex?
blocks.text: My pathway evidence: the three recorded browser intervals were 604, 661, 694 ms in original order, median 661 ms and range 90 ms. These are actual browser-test automation values for software review, not human performance data. Retinal/sensory input, brain processing, motor pathways and hand muscles contribute to the whole task. No nerve length or isolated conduction time was measured. The same pointer method/device was used; early presses are excluded rather than zero-filled. Attention and preparation may vary, as can display/input/software delays. Three repeated measurements describe this small run without proving an exact cause, population difference, reflex circuit or health/intelligence score.

blocks.prompt: Does the measured interval give the speed of one nerve signal?
blocks.text:
No. It includes several body processes and device delays; no nerve length was measured.
Correct! Reaction-task time is an interval, in ms. A signal speed needs distance and travel time for a defined pathway, not this whole response. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: Why is an early press not entered as a zero-millisecond response?
blocks.text:
It happened before the cue, so it does not measure a response to that cue.
Correct! Retain the early attempt as excluded evidence. Do not invent a response time or silently remove it. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: One of your three values is higher. What does this establish?
blocks.text:
This run varied. More controlled evidence is needed to identify the cause.
Correct! Attention, preparation, movement, software and hardware can vary. A small descriptive run does not isolate one cause. Correct on first recorded check.

The recorded values come from events in this browser, not a calibrated laboratory timer. Timing starts with the browser’s cue update and ends when its response handler runs. The exact moment light reaches your eyes is not measured. Display refresh, input hardware, software scheduling and any assistive announcement can add delays or variation. Showing a whole number of milliseconds does not guarantee one-millisecond accuracy. A very short value can include anticipation; this task cannot detect every guess. Perception, attention, preparation, brain processing, movement and device delays all contribute. Total task time is not a nerve-conduction speed, an intelligence score or a measure of nervous-system health. Three trials describe only this small run; they cannot separate causes of variation or establish a population effect. Practice, fatigue and order may matter. The pathway diagram is a broad explanation with many cells, connections and processing steps omitted. It is not a picture of exactly four neurons or a recording of signals inside your body. Real reflex pathways vary; this planned visual response should not be treated as a spinal reflex. No ruler-drop, clinical or electrical-testing procedure is supplied.
